content:
Chris Moon saw his first ghost at 7-years-old. 

It was a hot night, and he couldn’t sleep. Then, he looked up and saw an apparition of a little boy standing at the foot of his bed. 

This night marked the beginning of a new journey, one that would carry him to creating the largest paranormal magazine, a popular TV show and even being possessed four times: convincing his devout Catholic dad to believe what he saw that night. 

“It was absolutely terrifying,” Moon said about his first ghost-sighting. “Because he didn’t look like a ghost. He looked like a solid human being in front of me. And so I laid there all night, and I closed my eyes and opened my eyes, and he was still there the entire time.

“So when I went and told my dad in the morning, I was like, ‘There’s a ghost in my room.’ And he told me, ‘The only ghost is the Holy Ghost,’ and I was like, ‘I’m screwed.’”

This was far from the last haunting encounter from his childhood. Moon said there was a grand piano that would play by itself and doors that would open and shut at random in his childhood home. 

His father still didn’t believe him until much later on in life. 

Moon, professional paranormal investigator, visited Wichita State Wednesday night, 10 years since his last visit. 

“I will tell you, you have a very haunted campus,” Moon said. “And that’s the reason that I keep coming back.”

For around an hour, Moon told stories from his ghost-hunting adventures. He followed the lecture with a ghost-hunting tour of Wilner Auditorium and the McKnight Art Center for attendees who had RSVP’d prior. 

Moon became a musician, but wherever he went, paranormal activity seemed to follow him. So, naturally, he started investigating the places his band would perform.

“While we were on tour, I would investigate the places where we would be in each city, and it kept me out of trouble, so my band was happy,” he said. “… And it was a lot of fun.” 

Moon eventually retired from music, compiled all the evidence he had of the paranormal and opened up an online magazine called “Ghost Hunter Magazine.” The magazine’s popularity quickly grew, with a TV show coming out a few months later.

“It was a situation where it went from us having to beg people to go into their homes and their businesses to investigate, and pretty soon, they were begging us to come in and take a look at what was going on, so they could get on a TV show,” Moon said. 

With more popularity came a big change and Moon, along with his skeptic father, opened the largest paranormal magazine: “Haunted Times.” 

They also opened Ghost Hunter University, which is still around today, where they will take people into extremely haunted places — like the Lizzie Borden house or the Sallie house — and teach them how to become paranormal investigators.

In Moon’s own investigations, he is best known for his EVPs — electronic voice phenomena. This is how they can capture a ghost’s voice. Moon uses it to ask the ghosts questions, and has even helped cops to open back up a cold case using “para-forensics.”

“Believe it or not, we do work with law enforcement agencies on solving cold case crimes,” Moon said. “… In this property, there were two young girls, unfortunately, that were raped and murdered inside the location. And we were able to actually communicate with them with a police officer there, with a detective there. And the information that he got from that actually opened the cold case back up.”

Ghost hunting, however, isn’t always fun or safe. Despite Moon taking precautions during his investigations, he said he has been possessed four times. His most recent possession happened in New Orleans following Mardi Gras. 

“It was a spirit from the late 1700s who’d been wronged by the church,” Moon said. “They were very devout to the church, but the church didn’t like their practices, didn’t like who they were and ended up killing them. And that became possessed in middle ground, which then possessed me.

“And all I remember at the end was my mom taking me to a church, and me waking up in the middle of just divulging information, and tears pouring down my face. And it released me at that point. That possession was because that spirit had to put its story out.” 

Despite the dangers of ghost hunting, Moon still sees his affinity for the paranormal as a gift.

“What happens is that if you’re an open channel, if you’re a psychic, if you have abilities, you’re going to pick up on whatever it is that you run into,” Moon said. “… Pretty much anywhere that I go, I pick up on things. And I consider it a gift. Some people say that it’s a curse, but I think it’s a gift to be able to sense things and communicate with things. And the greatest reward is to help spirits cross over if they can.”

Moon has also been able to connect with other paranormal investigators, like Lorraine and Ed Warren, the couple “The Conjuring” movies are based upon.

“(She was) just an incredible human being,” Moon said. “The thing that I love about Lorriane is that who you saw publicly is who she was privately. She is probably sweeter behind the scenes. She really cared about the work, she cared about helping people. It was a huge loss when we lost her.” 

Years ago, Ed was in a coma due to an illness. Lorraine, Moon and the Warren’s nephew were in the hospital when Ed’s voice came through the voice box. He told their nephew to go grab a book where they found a note stashed in the pages, detailing what to do when he died. 

Moon said everyone was freaked out. This was the first time they had communicated with someone through the ghost box who wasn’t dead.

“When it was all said and done, I went out to the back porch,” he said. “And I was standing there just trying to catch my breath, and I turned to my left, and I saw Ed right there, right in front of me. And then he was gone.”

Ed Warren died later that week.

Throughout the lecture, Moon showed multiple photos, and played multiple audio clips and videos. One depicted the ghost of a confederate soldier standing in the grass of the Tomb of the Unmarked Soldier. One showed a demonic spirit floating behind a woman. And one video showed ghost orbs flying in the air. Moon said the parents filmed that video to prove to their kids that their imaginary friends weren’t real. 

“Kids see what’s there,” Moon said. “Animals see what’s there. It’s not until you get to about age 9 that your brain waves separate.” 

Moon also spoke about how the rise of artificial intelligence has made his job harder.

“AI has made my life completely impossible,” Moon said. “Because anything that’s put there right now, everybody claims AI. And I usually tell people if it’s too good to be true, it was probably AI. So I can only vouch for the things that I am able to go out and do now.”

These issues don’t mean the profession is dead, however. Two students at WSU said they are mediums and are looking to create their own ghost hunting channel. Communications science and disorders major Rebecca O’Toole said she has been seeing ghosts her entire life. 

“I actually live in a previously haunted house,” O’Toole said. “My family are the second owners of it. I routinely see the first owner checking in on the house. He loves what we do, what we’ve done with the house and how we made it our own home.”

O’Toole is deaf. Her friend Anne Yuengel, a forensic science major, said she is a lot more sensitive to paranormal noises. 

“We like to see it as her hearing is not only in tune with the physical world, it’s also in tune with the spiritual world,” Yuengel said.

The pair want to start their ghost hunting channel, Empathic Nightmares, for the same reason Moon started his.

Not everyone believes in ghosts, however. WSU students Emma Chaput and Ella Frazee attended the event because they were bored. Before the event, the pair created a bingo card with things they believed Moon would do and show during his lecture.

Things like “jump scare” and “picture of a ghost” were on the card. They had four bingos by the end of the presentation.

Chaput and Frazee also attended the ghost tour, complete with its own bingo card. This wasn’t their first ghost tour, though.

“I went to one in North Dakota,” Frazee said. “It was interesting. There was a lot of mirror usage.”

Chaput went to the Ohio State Reformatory with a group of coworkers. 

“They said I was attacked, but I don’t think I was,” she said. “I think I just scratched myself going up the attic or something. He was like, ‘You need to go to a priest.’ I was like, ‘I’m not going to a priest. Like, I’m fine, I promise.’”

Moon said he doesn’t really care about making every skeptic believe in ghosts. After all, he finally got his Catholic father to believe him.

“That’s why I started ghost hunting when I was a little kid,” Moon said. “It’s because I was trying to prove to my father I’m not crazy. This is real. And for him to finally admit it in an event that we did. He says, ‘He actually made me a believer; he actually showed me the reality of the situation.’ I was like, ‘Yes. Mission accomplished.’”

His father now runs the Capital Hill Ghost Tour and, according to Moon, is great at capturing ghost orbs.
